The Celsius scale originally defined the boiling point of water at one atmosphere as 100 °C, a standard established in 1743 by Jean-Pierre Christin when he reversed the thermometer scale to set freezing at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C. This assignment remains a foundational reference in temperature measurement.

The Celsius scale, as originally defined by Jean-Pierre Christin in 1743, assigns a boiling-point temperature of 100 °C to water at one atmosphere of pressure. This definition sets 0 °C as the freezing point of water and 100 °C as the boiling point under standard atmospheric conditions. Today, the Celsius scale is formally defined by the triple point of Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water, which is exactly 0.01 °C, but the original reference point for water’s boiling point remains 100 °C at 1 atm.
